SoloFactory 0.10 ← Back to SoloFactory

User manual

From a conversation to a running, verified app on your own machine. Your Codex or Claude subscription does the AI work; SoloFactory owns the process, the gates and the evidence.

1. Start the factory

You need Node 22 to 24 (Node 24 LTS recommended) and a signed-in Codex or Claude Code command line, on macOS or Linux. On Windows, SoloFactory runs inside the Ubuntu (WSL2) window: run every command there and open the address in your usual Windows browser. In an installed SoloFactory folder, start it with:

bash start.sh

(From a source checkout, npm start does the same.)

Open http://127.0.0.1:4173. The status pill top right reads Factory ready when a provider is signed in. No API key is ever asked for or stored; the agents run under your subscription. If another app already uses port 4173, the factory says so and stops; start it on a free port with PORT=5000 npm start and open http://127.0.0.1:5000 instead.

Updates

The factory tells you when a newer SoloFactory is out. The Check for updates button in the header, next to Manual, turns into a green Update available pill; click it to see both versions and the prompt to paste into Claude Code or Codex, with a Copy prompt button. Nothing covers your work and nothing updates on its own, so update when it suits you. It checks at startup, when you open or refresh the page, and when you click the button; never in the background. Offline, a manual check says Couldn't check. Screenshots: the update notice.

2. Projects

A project is the folder the factory builds into. The first selector in the header switches between them; New project… asks for a name in a small dialog. Each project is its own git repository with the app at the root, a .aai/ folder of project context you can edit, and a run history. .aai/review.md holds your own review rules (for example "money is stored in integer cents"); every reviewer checks the app against them.

In an installed SoloFactory folder, projects live in its projects/ folder (from a source checkout, under .solofactory/projects/). A folder you create there by hand shows up too. Switching projects never interrupts a run.

3. Shape the brief

The Brief page is where every brief is shaped, checked and queued: a new idea, an interview you left unfinished, and a revision of an earlier run. The brief reads as a document on the left. The Factory Guide sits in a sidebar on the right and stays in view as you scroll.

Answer in your own words in the box at the bottom of the Guide. Enter sends; Shift+Enter adds a line. The Guide keeps asking until all 13 topics are covered, from the promise and the primary user to the acceptance scenarios and the constraints. The queue button counts them (Brief not ready · 4 of 13) and stays off until the brief is complete, because a vague brief is the most expensive kind of bug.

Already have a spec? Use Attach in the Guide box. Markdown, text, JSON, YAML and CSV files go into the conversation as your turn, and the Guide reads the whole document. Attach a png, jpg, gif or webp mockup and the Guide opens it before answering; images are saved inside the project under .factory/uploads/. There is no per-message length limit, and long pastes fold up in the conversation with a Show full message link.

View and Edit. The switch in the bar over the page changes only how you work on the brief, never how the Guide treats your messages. In View you read the brief and tell the Guide what to change. In Edit you click a section (or Tab to it and press Enter) and rewrite it yourself, one line per item for a list. Leave the section, or press Cmd/Ctrl+Enter, to keep the edit; Esc cancels it. The Guide then checks your edit against the rest of the brief. It keeps your wording, says if anything conflicts, and while topics are still open asks its next question as usual. If a later answer of the Guide's leaves your text out, SoloFactory puts it back; only when the Guide writes something new for that section, for example because you asked it to, does its text replace yours.

Every run plans its features first. There is no strategy to pick. Before any code is written the factory drafts a feature plan, and an independent review has to pass it. Each feature then declares the files it creates or edits (its writes), is built, tested, reviewed and committed before the next starts, and may change only those files. Features fail smaller than one big build, and a parked run can be restarted from a chosen feature.

Checks the factory can prove. The factory can only prove what a test can run on its own. When a check needs a real folder on your computer, a real calendar date or a live outside service, the Guide rewrites it to use sample files, a test clock, a setting for the folder (such as <DocsRoot>) or a stand-in. What only a person can confirm goes in a Checked by hand after install section of the brief and in the PRD. On Windows the app runs inside Ubuntu, so a folder like D:\Docs is /mnt/d/Docs to it; that is the value to give the folder setting. A check that needs hours or days of real time or media (recordings up to 6 hours, delete after 30 days) becomes a short sample or a test clock, with the long limit kept as a setting.

Everything saves on its own. There is no save button. The brief is saved after every Guide answer and every edit, and a message you have typed but not sent is saved a moment after you stop typing, so closing the tab loses nothing: reopen the page and it comes back. The status line in the bar says what state it is in (Saved 1:37 PM · not submitted, Saved · message not sent yet, Ready · the Guide reviews it when you queue). Start over under the Guide box clears the draft, and queuing the brief deletes it.

Anything the Guide could not resolve, and a brief with more than 12 checks (each one costs its own build, test and review turns), shows as a note under Before you queue at the top of the brief. Read those before you queue it.

On a phone the Guide folds into a rail at the right edge. Tap Guide to open it over the brief and Hide to close it.

4. Queue a run

Queue for the factory starts with a final review. The Guide reads the exact brief that would be frozen, your own edits included, against the interview checklist, so that everything downstream is built from a brief that is clear and complete. It sizes the change first: a narrow change to an earlier run (one rule, screen, field or message, with no new data, integration, flow or architecture) gets a one-line confirmation; a wider one gets the full check.

  • Nothing missing: the brief freezes and the run joins the project's queue. You land back on a fresh brief, so you can shape the next release while this one builds.
  • A question: nothing is queued. The Guide asks it in the sidebar; answer, then press Queue again.
  • The review adjusted the brief: nothing is queued. The changed sections are marked; check them and press Queue again, which queues without a second review.
  • The review kept leaving out one of your edits: the button becomes Queue anyway, so queuing the brief as shown takes one deliberate click.

The review costs one Guide turn. A brief the Guide has already reviewed exactly as it stands queues at once; any edit or answer after that means a fresh review. The button also names what queuing does to a stopped run: Queue and replace run …, Queue and set aside run …, or Queue as a new run after a finished one. If a different stopped run holds the project by the time you press it, nothing is queued: the button changes to name what queuing now does, and pressing it again queues.

  • Runs in one project go one after another, each building on the tree the last one left. A note at the end of a ready brief says so when the project already has a run active, queued, or parked, since independent fixes for one app are cheaper as a single brief.
  • Runs in different projects can overlap when SOLOFACTORY_MAX_ACTIVE_RUNS is above 1.
  • A second brief for a project that already shipped becomes a follow-on release. The previous release keeps running until the new one passes its checks, then stops. If the new release fails to deploy, the previous one stays up and the run's card says where; if it is not running, the card offers Dismiss, then Relaunch to put it back.
  • Remove from queue drops a brief that has not started.

5. Follow a run

The second header selector picks a run within the current project. The run view shows:

PanelWhat it tells you
Run mapThe plan as a metro line, one numbered stop per feature, with a health pill, the selected stop, four status answers and the activity stream. Details below.
Live app activityAggregate metrics from the deployed app: requests, errors, latency, uptime and route counts. No bodies, headers, addresses or identifiers. It also shows the URL the app is on. After a restart of SoloFactory the app is no longer running: the card says so, and Relaunch app starts it again on a fresh port (newest run in the project only).
ArtifactsProduct requirements, build plan, acceptance contract, frozen input, slice plan, runtime manifest, and Open working app once it is live.

The rail on the left shows the six stages. Each one ends with a gate the controller owns: install, test and build (and lint, when the app declares one) must exit 0; review must pass; the deployed app must answer its health check and serve a non-empty home page. A failed gate gets at most two bounded repair attempts per feature, then the run parks. At final integration a test or proof check that fails is first rerun once, at no repair cost: if it passes, the activity stream says failed, then passed when rerun, and the final review checks it as a likely race.

The run map

  • Stops. The title names the plan (Feature plan, or Repair plan during a recovery) and its feature count. A green stop is verified, an orange stop is the one being built, a grey stop with a dotted line has not been reached, and a red stop is where the run stopped or paused. A small badge on the orange stop shows how long it has been running. Before a plan exists, the map shows five pipeline stops instead: SPEC, BUILD, GATES, REVIEW, DEPLOY.
  • Click a stop (or focus it and press Enter) to read about it. A finished feature shows its exact time, its repairs and how its review went, for example Verified · 12m 05s · no repairs · review passed first try; sub-minute steps read like 45s. That time is the wall-clock gap since the previous feature was verified, so a pause counts. The current feature shows its time so far and its repairs used. A feature not reached yet names what it waits on. Selecting a stop also draws orange dotted curves to the features it depends on.
  • Health pill. Alive while the agent or its commands were active in the last 10 minutes, Quiet in amber up to 30 minutes and red beyond, Running <check> while a test or proof gate runs, and Stopped · needs you, Paused · needs you, Queued or Finished. Click it for the explanation.
  • Needs-you banner. When any project’s latest run is stopped or paused, an amber banner names it on every screen and the browser tab reads (N) needs you. Open jumps to that run.
  • Four or five answers sit under the map. Moving? says whether work is happening and what happened last. Healthy? shows repairs used (on this feature and in the whole plan during a recovery) and how many acceptance cases pass. How far? counts verified features, estimates the time left from the average finished feature, and gives the run's total time and tokens. Needs you? says No or names the one thing to do, such as approving a repair plan. When Resume is the step, a fifth answer, Safe to resume?, says whether the stop was a limit rather than an error (usage window, spending limit, provider outage, or your pause) and counts the features verified and new checks passed since your last Resume. If a Resume bought nothing, it says Not yet and points you to Report this run.
  • Activity stream. Every lifecycle event, newest first, with filters for All, Agent, Files, Gates and Stages. Gate results, commits, agent starts and stops.

6. The Factory board

Factory in the header opens the board. Columns follow the lifecycle: queued, specifying, building, reviewing, deploying, then parked and completed. Repairing counts as building; failed, interrupted, cancelled and paused runs all sit in parked. Each card names its project, stage and duration, and slice runs carry a progress bar. A queued card that is waiting on a parked run says so.

Click a card to open that run. If it belongs to another project the factory switches to it first.

7. Pause, resume, cancel, restart

ControlWhen it showsWhat it does
PauseWhile a stage is runningLets the run finish the stage it is in, commits the green tree, and parks before the next one. The button reads Pausing after … until the run parks, also after a page reload. No new agent turn starts once you press it: a failed check, a blocked review or a blocked plan parks before its repair or correction, and Resume picks that up without re-running the review. Pausing while a repair plan is being prepared stops that preparation; prepare the plan again to continue. Nothing is lost and nothing is replayed on resume.
ResumeOn a paused, failed or interrupted run, when the recovery card allows itContinues the same run, same files, from the stage it stopped at. Goes to the front of the project's queue. It does not renew a spent repair budget; when the budget is spent the card offers Prepare repair plan instead. One exception: after an update, a check that failed on the older SoloFactory shows Resume with SoloFactory changed since this gate failed; Resume reruns that check on the new version first, at no model cost, and only a repeat failure leads to a repair plan.
Cancel runWhile activeStops work now. The workspace stays as it was.
Restart from sliceOn a parked run, for every completed feature after the firstRewinds the tree to the commit before that slice and rebuilds it and everything after, exactly once. Earlier slices keep their commits.
Prepare repair plan, Approve and continue repairsOn a parked run that cannot simply resumePlans the unfinished work as repair features; see When a run parks. The recovery card offers this instead of Resume when Resume would only hit the same wall.
Start overOn a parked runCreates a brand-new run from the same brief and sets the parked one aside. Use it when the first feature itself is wrong.
Revise briefOn a stopped or finished runOpens the run's brief on the Brief page, in Edit mode, with the run's stop reason at the top of the Guide and an Open the run link. Tell the Guide what to change, or rewrite sections yourself; sections that differ from the run's brief are marked and the bar counts them. Earlier interview messages fold under N earlier messages. The revision saves as you go; come back to it with Continue saved revision on the same run. Queuing runs the final review and then starts a new run from the revised brief. If a stopped run is holding the project's queue, the brief says so first and queuing sets that run aside, rolling back its files; a finished run is never rolled back. Only one revision is kept at a time, so starting another one asks you to click twice.
DismissOn a parked runSets this run aside and releases the project's queue. If the app shipped before, it goes back to that release; its saved records are kept.

8. When a run parks

A run parks when a gate fails past its repair budget, a check’s test runner crashes after every test passed (no repair is spent on that), an agent hits a usage limit, sign-in, network or toolchain problem, the factory restarts mid-run, or you pause or cancel it. Known blockers are never blindly retried; a parked run holds its project's queue so nothing builds on a half-repaired tree.

The Recovery checkpoint card explains what happened, what to do, where the preserved files are, and whether any automatic retry was spent (the Token safeguard line). Copy recovery packet puts a full handoff on your clipboard for pasting into Codex or Claude when you want to fix things by hand, then Resume from the preserved workspace.

A feature that keeps failing

  • Set aside. When a feature runs out of repairs, the factory saves its work aside and keeps building every later feature that does not depend on it. Features that do depend on it wait, and the activity stream says so. Because every feature declares its writes, the independent work does not collide with the set-aside files. This only happens when later independent work remains. At the end the run parks once, with the set-aside feature's own files restored and its unspent repairs given back; the message lists which features were built and which are still waiting.
  • Repair plan. When Resume would only repeat the failure (repairs spent, the same failure on unchanged code, a feature that never reached a stable review, or specs changed), the card offers Prepare repair plan. The factory plans the unfinished work as repair features from the review findings and every spec and prototype input; each feature lists the checks it closes, what it depends on and the files it writes. An independent review has to pass the plan, and then repairs start on their own. The card shows the features (verified, current, pending), a strip with one cell per feature, and the checks still open. Add a spec or prototype file, or type Changes for the repair plan, before preparing it if the inputs need correcting.
  • If you pause while the plan is being prepared, a plan that passed review waits for Approve and continue repairs. A preparation that stopped or failed offers Retry repair-plan preparation; a plan still blocked after its automatic corrections offers Submit corrected plan for review (a .json file under Advanced, with a Download plan help packet to help write it) or Revise inputs and prepare a new plan if the specs themselves are wrong.
  • Repair budget. Each feature gets two repair attempts and the final full review gets two more; spent attempts are never refilled by Resume, Retry or a restart. The card shows Repair attempts used: This feature 1 of 2 · Plan: 3 of 8 while repairs run. A first gate failure gets a repair plan for the failed feature only.
  • What it has spent. Every parked run shows Spent so far (workers, tokens, cost and time), how many repair turns approving grants, and how many recent approvals verified no features, so you can decide before you approve more.
  • Spending ceilings. A run that has started 150 workers parks as Run worker ceiling reached; one that Claude reports has cost about $30 parks as Run cost ceiling reached (on a subscription that is list price, not a bill: it tracks how fast the run uses your weekly limit); one whose agents reported about 40M tokens parks as Run token ceiling reached, which also holds on Codex. Nothing is lost; review the spend and Resume to grant another allotment. SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_WORKERS, SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_COST_USD and SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_TOKENS change the ceilings.
  • Resume, Retry or Start over? Resume continues the approved repair plan from the feature it stopped on, never replaying verified ones. Retry (of plan preparation) keeps the prior plan and the features already built. Start over makes a new run from the same brief and sets the parked one aside.

Release QA

After the last feature, the final review looks at what no single feature review could see: how features work together, whether the app is ready to deploy, and security (input checks, file paths, committed secrets, unsafe login defaults). That reviewer reports defects and does not fix feature code. For each defect it writes a failing test under qa/, and the factory hands the defect to the feature that owns the broken files for repair. At final integration the whole test suite runs, every built feature's proofs rerun, and so does every qa/ test, including those from earlier releases, so a fixed bug stays fixed.

When a prompt is too big

No prompt sent to an agent may exceed 200,000 characters; large inputs go into files the agent reads. If one ever does, the run parks with over SoloFactory's 200000-character prompt limit and no agent starts. This is a factory defect, not something your brief caused. The same build would build the same prompt again, so the card offers no Resume or Retry until a different SoloFactory build is running. Use Report this run and install the fix.

9. Report a problem

Feedback in the header, or Report this run on a parked run, drafts a bug report or feature request. The run report attaches the run's evidence and the last log lines, scrubbed of paths and secrets. The body always travels through your clipboard, so you see exactly what is sent. Choose Preview report, then Copy & open email: it copies the report and opens a message to support@coachlou.com with the subject "SoloFactory Feedback" — paste the report into the body and send.

Every error along the way is also written to errors.jsonl in the factory's home folder: failed requests, failed runs, errors shown in the browser, and failed calls the chat agent makes. Paths and secrets are scrubbed first. The file stays on your machine; /api/errors shows the latest entries, and the agent reads them when you report a problem.

10. Settings

VariableMeaning
SOLOFACTORY_HOMEWhere runs, projects and the demo live. Default .solofactory/ inside the SoloFactory folder (installed folders use .aai/memory/solofactory/).
SOLOFACTORY_ROOTWhere projects are discovered. Default: the home.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_ACTIVE_RUNSHow many projects may build at once. Default 1.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_WORKERSWorkers one run may start before it parks for your go-ahead (Resume grants another allotment). Default 150; 0 turns the ceiling off.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_COST_USDDollars of Claude-reported cost one run may spend before it parks for your go-ahead (Resume grants another allotment). Default 30; 0 turns the ceiling off. Codex reports no cost, so a Codex run is held by the token and worker ceilings.
SOLOFACTORY_MAX_RUN_TOKENSTokens (input, cached included, plus output) one run may use before it parks for your go-ahead (Resume grants another allotment). Default 40,000,000; 0 turns the ceiling off. Both Claude and Codex report tokens, so this ceiling holds on Codex too.
SOLOFACTORY_UPDATE_CHECKSet to 0 to turn off the check for a newer SoloFactory release. Default on.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_MODELClaude model for builders and repairs. Default sonnet.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_EFFORTClaude effort for builders and repairs. Default medium.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_REASONING_MODELClaude model for planning, plan review, correction and reviews. Default opus.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_REASONING_EFFORTClaude effort for planning, plan review, correction and reviews. Default low.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_GUIDE_MODELClaude model for the Guide interview. Default opus.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_GUIDE_EFFORTClaude effort for the Guide interview. Default medium.
SOLOFACTORY_CLAUDE_GUIDE_ADVISORAdvisor model the Guide can consult. Default opus; set it empty to turn the advisor off.
SOLOFACTORY_CODEX_MODELCodex model for every stage. Default gpt-6.1-sol.
SOLOFACTORY_CODEX_REASONING_EFFORTCodex reasoning effort. Default medium.
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_IDLE_MINUTESAgent idle deadline, reset by any output. Default 6.
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_HARD_MINUTESAgent total safety cap. Default 45.
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_BACKOFF_SECONDSWait before the one automatic Codex resume. Default 15.
SOLOFACTORY_PROGRESS_MINUTESShow "Progress needs checking" when a busy worker lands no gate, commit or approved plan for this long. A warning only; nothing is stopped. Default 20, 0–240, 0 turns it off.
SOLOFACTORY_LOOP_THRESHOLDStop repairing after this many identical failures on unchanged code. Default 3, 2–10.
SOLOFACTORY_SYMPTOM_THRESHOLDStop repairing after this many identical failures even though repairs changed the code (line numbers ignored). Default 4, 0–20, 0 turns it off.
SOLOFACTORY_AGENT_MAX_TURNSTool steps one Claude turn may take before it stops with agent_turn_cap. Default 150, 0–1000, 0 turns it off.
SOLOFACTORY_GATE_MINUTESHard limit for each test or proof gate; install always gets at least 10. A gate that runs out parks the run without a repair turn. Default 5, 1–60.
SOLOFACTORY_DEMO=1Run with the deterministic fixture provider instead of a real agent.
SOLOFACTORY_ISSUES_URLWhere feedback reports are filed.

11. Work from Claude Code or Codex

You don't have to use the browser. Open Claude Code or Codex in your SoloFactory folder and say "hey solofactory". The agent checks where your apps stand, tells you in a sentence, and ends every reply with numbered options. Answer with a number or in your own words.

You:   hey solofactory

Agent: Your habit tracker is live at http://127.0.0.1:49762.
       Nothing is building right now.

       1. Add or change features in the habit tracker
       2. Start a new app
       3. Open the habit tracker
       4. Report a problem with the factory

You:   1 — I want reminders, a streak counter, and dark mode

Agent: Got it, three changes. A few quick questions...
       Here's the plan: ... This uses your subscription.

       1. Go, build it
       2. Change something first

You:   1

Agent: Queued. ... Reminders are built and passed their checks (1 of 3).
       ... Done. All three work: http://127.0.0.1:49762

The options change with where you are, and Report a problem with the factory is always the last one:

Where you areWhat you're offered
No apps yetStart my first app · How does this work?
An app is liveAdd or change features · Start a new app · Open it
A build is runningHow far along is it? · Show me the plan · Pause it · Stop it
A build stopped with a problemWhat went wrong? · Pick up where it stopped · Go back to an earlier feature · Set it aside
More than one appWhich app? · Start a new app
  • Ask for several features at once. They go in as one request. The factory builds them one at a time and checks each before starting the next, so nothing reaches you untested.
  • Nothing costs you without a yes. The agent shows the plan and builds only after you say go. It also asks before pausing, stopping, or fixing a run.
  • Only real options. If you ask for something the factory can't do, the agent says so and shows your options again.
  • Reporting a problem. The agent asks what happened, drafts the same scrubbed report as the Feedback button, and tells you to email it to support@coachlou.com with the subject "SoloFactory Feedback". It never sends anything itself.

A build started from the chat also shows up on the Factory board, and you can switch between the chat and the browser at any time.

Folder set up before version 0.9.1? Its instructions still point the agent at the browser, so the first time say "hey solofactory — work from the chat, following SoloFactory's drive.md."

Screenshots were taken from the demo mode (fixture provider), which is why every project is called Pocket Pulse.
